newsitem.title: USA: Miss. municipalities sue over electric service.
newsitem.headline: Miss. municipalities sue over electric service.

text.p: Eleven municipalities asked the Mississippi Supreme Court to overturn a law barring them from providing electric service to annexed areas without approval from the state Public Service Commission, a newspaper said.
The Northeast Mississippi Daily Journal said the Mississippi Supreme Court heard oral arguments in the case on Wednesday. The court did not indicate when it would rule.
At issue is whether municipalities have the right to declare eminent domain and take over part of a service area of an electric power association member or a private utility company.

Under a 1987 law that passed despite a veto by Gov. Bill Allen, the municipalities cannot expand. Instead, they must go before the Public Service Commission and ask them to revoke the premit that allows the electric power association or utility to serve the area.
"If the power companies are providing adequate service, then the Public Service Commission's hands are tied," said attorney T.H. Freeland, who represented municipalities including Oxford and Tupelo.
Freeland said no municipality has ever taken such a request to the commission because the law makes it so difficult for the commission to act.
He argued that the law is unconstitutional because it restricts municipalities' eminent domain authority to take land at a fair price for the public good.

Larry Moffett, representing the Rural Power Associations of Mississippi, said the municipalities have that authority only because they were given it by the Legislature, which has the authority to restrict how they can use it.
"The proper jurisdiction for this (argument) is in the Legislature, not in the courts," Moffett told the Supreme Court.
The City of Oxford appealed the case to the state Supreme Court after it lost a legal challenge in circuit court in October.
Freeland said 25 percent of Oxford is served by an electric power association, but that the city could provide the service to the area at less cost and more efficiently.

Hobson Waits, executive vice president of the Electric Power Assoications of Mississippi, said it would be unfair to give the service areas to municipalities after rural electric associations had established service and built the infrastructure.
